pos: n. pl. (the hubs of wheels; the central blocks into which the spokes are set)
etymology: From Old English nafu, the hub of a wheel, related to navel as the central point. Not to be confused with the nave of a church, which comes from Latin navis, a ship. The Hebrew gab here means the back or boss of a wheel.
biblical_def: In the inventory of Solomon's temple furnishings the brasen bases for the lavers are described down to the parts of their wheels: “And the work of the wheels was like the work of a chariot wheel: their axletrees, and their naves, and their felloes, and their spokes, were all molten” (1 Kings 7:33). The naves are the hubs, the central blocks into which the spokes are set and through which the axle runs. Four parts are named, and the last clause is the point: they were all molten, cast in brass rather than assembled from pieces. Nothing was improvised. Scripture spends whole chapters on brass hubs and sockets because the house of God was built by pattern and not by preference, and the same care appears in the parallel notice of the bases themselves: “And every base had four brasen wheels, and plates of brass” (1 Kings 7:30). Ezekiel saw wheels of another order altogether in his vision by Chebar, “as it were a wheel in the middle of a wheel” (Ezekiel 1:16), where the mobility of God's throne answers the fixed furniture of the temple. The nave is the small word that holds the wheel together.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): NAVE, the thick piece of timber in the centre of a wheel, in which the spokes are inserted; the hub.
webster_full: NAVE, n. The thick piece of timber in the center of a wheel, in which the spokes are inserted.

corruption_summary: The detailed building inventories of Scripture are dismissed as tedious archival padding, when they exist to teach that God's house is built by His pattern and not by the builder's taste.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the one the inventory chapters exist to press: the house of God was built to a revealed pattern, down to the hubs of the laver wheels, and the builders had no liberty to improve on it.

The modern habit is to skip these chapters, or to treat them as the work of a later archivist with an interest in temple furniture. Both readings lose the doctrine. Moses was shewn a pattern in the mount and warned to make all things according to it; David gave Solomon the pattern by the Spirit; and the result is a text that records brass naves because obedience in small things is obedience. The regulative principle of worship is not a Puritan invention but the plain logic of 1 Kings 7.

pos: n. pl. (the bars radiating from the hub of a wheel to its rim)
etymology: From Old English spaca, a spoke, related to spike and to Dutch speek. A spoke is a radiating bar. The Hebrew chishshur denotes the joining pieces of a wheel.
biblical_def: The same verse that gives us naves gives us spokes: “And the work of the wheels was like the work of a chariot wheel: their axletrees, and their naves, and their felloes, and their spokes, were all molten” (1 Kings 7:33). Spokes are the bars that run from hub to rim, and in a working wheel they are the parts that bear the load. The comparison the text draws is instructive: these temple wheels were made like the work of a chariot wheel, that is, to the best standard of the most demanding craft of the age. Solomon did not furnish the house of God with ornamental imitations but with brass cast to the strength of war machinery. The spoke is also a figure that preaches itself: every bar set into one hub, every bar bearing in its turn, no bar bearing alone. Ezekiel's living wheels, “a wheel in the middle of a wheel” (Ezekiel 1:16), carry the throne of God in any direction without turning; the temple wheels carried water for the washing of sacrifices. Both testify that God's service is a service that moves.

corruption_summary: Craftsmanship in the service of God is treated as a lesser calling than speech or office, when Scripture records the names of workmen and the strength of their castings.
corruption_paragraphs: This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the dignity of the workman in the house of God. The text pauses over hubs, felloes and spokes, and names Hiram of Tyre who cast them, because skilled work offered to God is not a support service to the ministry but a part of the worship.

The church has often inverted this, treating the visible platform as the real calling and the trades as what pays for it. Scripture says of Bezaleel that God filled him with the spirit of God in all manner of workmanship, and of the temple wheels that they were made to the standard of a chariot wheel. The brass was cast to bear weight. A congregation that honours its craftsmen as Exodus and 1 Kings honour theirs is reading its Bible rightly.

pos: n. pl. (raised walks or stairways; here, structures of algum wood in the temple and palace)
etymology: From Old French terrace, from Latin terra, earth: a raised level place or walk. The Hebrew mesillah means a raised way, a causeway or stair, from salal, to cast up a highway.
biblical_def: The algum timber that Huram's servants brought from Ophir was put to a particular use: “And the king made of the algum trees terraces to the house of the LORD, and to the king's palace, and harps and psalteries for singers: and there were none such seen before in the land of Judah” (2 Chronicles 9:11). Terraces renders a Hebrew word for a raised way or stair, so the finest imported timber in Judah was spent on the approach to the house of God and on the instruments of its praise. The parallel in Kings says pillars where Chronicles says terraces, the two words describing different parts of one work: “And the king made of the almug trees pillars for the house of the LORD” (1 Kings 10:12). What both accounts agree in is the destination. The ships came back from Ophir laden with gold and precious stones and this rare wood (2 Chronicles 9:10), and the wood went to the temple first. A kingdom at the height of its wealth is tested by where the best of it goes, and in Solomon's best years it went up the stairs toward the house of the LORD.

corruption_summary: The difference between Kings and Chronicles at this verse is cited as proof of a contradictory Bible, when the two words describe different parts of a single work.
corruption_paragraphs: Where Chronicles says terraces Kings says pillars, and the pair is a stock item in lists of alleged biblical contradictions, often attached to the wider claim that Chronicles is a late and theologically motivated rewriting of Kings. The dictionary rejects both the charge and the framework. The Hebrew word in Chronicles means a raised way, and the word in Kings means supports; a stair of approach has both, and the two inspired historians record different members of the same structure.

What the texts agree in is the thing that matters and the thing least often noticed: the best timber in the kingdom went to the house of the LORD and to the instruments of praise. Inerrancy is not threatened by two true descriptions of one staircase. It would be threatened by a Bible that recorded the wealth of Ophir and said nothing about where it was spent.

pos: n. pl. (ornamental bosses or knobs, here of silver set in a bridal ornament)
etymology: From Old English studu, a post or prop, which came to mean an ornamental boss or knob set in a surface. The Hebrew nequddah means a point, bead or spangle, from a root meaning to mark with points.
biblical_def: In the first dialogue of the Song, the daughters of Jerusalem answer the bride's beloved with a promise of ornament: “We will make thee borders of gold with studs of silver” (Song of Solomon 1:11). Studs are bosses or beads, little points of silver set into a golden band, and the verse answers the one before it: “Thy cheeks are comely with rows of jewels, thy neck with chains of gold” (Song of Solomon 1:10). The bride, who has just confessed herself black because the sun had looked upon her, is being adorned rather than corrected. That is the pattern the dictionary reads throughout the Song: a real marriage, celebrated in the plainest terms, and in its figure the love of Christ for His church. Christ does not find a beautiful bride; He makes one, washing her with water by the word and presenting her to Himself without spot. The silver studs set in gold are therefore no trifle. They are what the Beloved's friends do for a bride who had nothing to bring, and the church sings the Song as a wife who was given her ornaments.

webster_full: STUD, n. A nail with a large head, driven chiefly for ornament; a boss.

A post or prop; the original Old English sense.

corruption_summary: The Song is read either as mere erotic anthology with no reference to Christ, or allegorised until the real marriage it celebrates disappears.
corruption_paragraphs: Modern criticism generally treats the Song as a collection of Near Eastern love lyrics, denying Solomonic authorship and any typological reference. The dictionary holds Solomonic authorship and holds that the Song is what it says it is: the celebration of covenant marriage between one man and one woman, in the plainest and most unembarrassed language in Scripture.

The opposite error, common in some older preaching, allegorises every detail until the bride's cheeks and the silver studs become doctrines and the marriage vanishes. Scripture itself forbids that erasure, since Paul grounds the mystery of Christ and the church in a real one-flesh union. Hold both and the verse keeps its force: a bride is adorned by her beloved's gift, and the church reads her own story in it.

pos: adj. (of the thyine tree; a fragrant, costly North African citron wood)
etymology: From Greek thuinos, of the thuia tree, related to thuo, to sacrifice or burn incense, because the wood was aromatic when burned. Roman writers call it citrus; it is the citron wood of Mauretania, prized above all woods for tables.
biblical_def: The lament over Babylon's fallen trade lists her cargoes one by one: “The merchandise of gold, and silver, and precious stones, and of pearls, and fine linen, and purple, and silk, and scarlet, and all thyine wood, and all manner vessels of ivory, and all manner vessels of most precious wood, and of brass, and iron, and marble” (Revelation 18:12). Thyine wood is the citron wood of North Africa, the most extravagant luxury in the Roman furniture trade; a single table of it could cost a senator's fortune, and the Romans wrote about the mania for it as a byword of excess. John's inventory is therefore a precise piece of economic observation as well as prophecy. It begins with gold and ends, two verses later, with “slaves, and souls of men” — the same list, the same market. That is the indictment: a commerce that treats a fragrant table and a human being as line items of the same ledger. And the end of it is sudden: “For in one hour so great riches is come to nought” (Revelation 18:17), while “the merchants of the earth shall weep and mourn over her” (Revelation 18:11).

webster_full: THYINE WOOD, a fragrant wood, mentioned in Revelation 18:12.

corruption_summary: Revelation 18 is read as a protest against commerce as such, or else spiritualised until it indicts nobody, when John's own list fixes the charge precisely.
corruption_paragraphs: Liberation-theological readings turn Revelation 18 into a condemnation of markets and private wealth in general, and the chapter is then used to baptise an economic programme. Scripture does not condemn trade: it honours the industrious, blesses the diligent hand, and fills Proverbs with commerce rightly conducted. The error on the other side is to spiritualise Babylon so thoroughly that no actual practice is ever named.

John names the practice himself by where his list ends. Thyine wood, ivory, marble, cinnamon, wheat, beasts, sheep, horses, chariots, and then slaves and souls of men, all in one unbroken inventory. The sin is a commerce that has lost the distinction between a fragrant table and a man made in God's image, and that has made luxury the end of life. In one hour it comes to nought. That is a judgment on a specific sin, not a theory of economics.

pos: n. (archaic spelling of instructor; a teacher, one who trains others in a craft)
etymology: From Latin instruere, to build in, to equip, to teach, from in and struere, to pile or build. The -er spelling was standard in older English and in Webster. The Hebrew lataš means to sharpen or whet, hence to forge.
biblical_def: The line of Cain is traced through its inventors, and the third is a metalworker: “And Zillah, she also bare Tubalcain, an instructer of every artificer in brass and iron: and the sister of Tubalcain was Naamah” (Genesis 4:22). An instructer is a teacher, and the point is not simply that Tubalcain worked metal but that he taught others to. Technology enters Scripture as a transmitted craft, with a master and apprentices. His brother is named in the same breath: “And his brother's name was Jubal: he was the father of all such as handle the harp and organ” (Genesis 4:21). Music and metallurgy, the arts and the trades, both arise in the line of Cain, and Scripture reports it without embarrassment and without applause. These are genuine goods, common graces given to a fallen race, and the chapter that records them also records Lamech's boast of murder with a weapon. The gifts are real and the heart is unchanged. The same crafts in covenant hands build a tabernacle, for God filled Bezaleel “with the spirit of God, in wisdom, and in understanding, and in knowledge, and in all manner of workmanship” (Exodus 31:3).

corruption_summary: Technical and artistic skill is treated either as proof of human progress apart from God or as worldly and suspect, when Scripture names it a common grace that the heart still governs.
corruption_paragraphs: Two errors meet in Genesis 4:22. The first is the myth of progress: because the Cainites invented metallurgy and music, civilisation is read as mankind's self-improvement, with religion a vestige it has outgrown. The chapter answers it in the next verses, where Lamech boasts of killing a man and of avenging himself seventy and sevenfold. The forge that made tools made weapons, and the maker's heart was not mended by his skill.

The second error is a pious suspicion of craft and culture altogether, as though the arts were tainted by their first practitioners. Scripture refuses that too. The same brass and iron, and the same harp, are used by God's command in tabernacle and temple, and the first man said to be filled with the Spirit of God in Scripture is a craftsman. Skill is a gift of common grace; whether it builds an altar or forges a weapon is a question about the man, not the trade.

pos: adj. (made of wheat; of wheat flour)
etymology: From wheat, Old English hwaete, with the material suffix -en as in wooden and golden. The Hebrew phrase is soleth chittim, fine flour of wheats.
biblical_def: In the ordinance for consecrating Aaron and his sons, the bread that accompanies the sacrifices is specified exactly: “And unleavened bread, and cakes unleavened tempered with oil, and wafers unleavened anointed with oil: of wheaten flour shalt thou make them” (Exodus 29:2). Wheaten flour is flour of wheat, and the specification excludes the cheaper barley that was the bread of the poor and of animals. Three forms are named — bread, cakes tempered with oil, wafers anointed with oil — and all three unleavened, since leaven pictures the spreading corruption of sin. The same requirement governs the meat offering generally: “his offering shall be of fine flour; and he shall pour oil upon it, and put frankincense thereon” (Leviticus 2:1). Fine wheaten flour is grain that has been threshed, winnowed, ground and sifted; nothing is brought to God raw. All of it is shadow. The true bread was not baked but given: “I am the bread of life: he that cometh to me shall never hunger” (John 6:35), and the grain of wheat that falls into the ground and dies is Christ's own figure for Himself.

webster_full: WHEATEN, a. Made of wheat; as wheaten bread.

corruption_summary: The precision of the ceremonial law is dismissed as priestly fussiness, so that the shadow is thrown away before the substance it pointed to is seen.
corruption_paragraphs: The documentary hypothesis assigns chapters like Exodus 29 to a Priestly source composed centuries after Moses to secure the privileges of a priestly class, and on that account the requirement of wheaten flour is institutional self-interest rather than divine command. The dictionary holds Mosaic authorship and the plain claim of the text: the LORD spake unto Moses, and these are His words.

A gentler version of the same error is common in churches that do believe the text. The ceremonial chapters are skipped as obsolete detail, and with them goes the whole typological structure that teaches us to read Christ. Fine wheaten flour, unleavened, tempered with oil, is a portrait: the sinless humanity of the Son, anointed with the Spirit, ground fine in His sufferings, offered without corruption. Lose the shadow and the substance is harder to see.

pos: n. (breadth; the measure of a space across)
etymology: From wide, Old English wid, with the suffix -ness. The Hebrew rochab means breadth, from rachab, to be broad.
biblical_def: In the long measuring of Ezekiel's temple vision, one dimension is given this name: “And between the chambers was the wideness of twenty cubits round about the house on every side” (Ezekiel 41:10). Wideness is simply breadth, and it is worth an entry because of the work the measuring does in these chapters. Ezekiel is shown the house by a man with a line of flax and a measuring reed, and the command given him is explicit: “behold with thine eyes, and hear with thine ears, and set thine heart upon all that I shall shew thee; for to the intent that I might shew them unto thee art thou brought hither: declare all that thou seest to the house of Israel” (Ezekiel 40:4). The purpose of the measurements is then stated: “shew the house to the house of Israel, that they may be ashamed of their iniquities: and let them measure the pattern” (Ezekiel 43:10). The exactness is the message. A people who had defiled a temple are given a house measured to the cubit, with a fixed wideness between the chambers, and told to measure the pattern. Holiness has dimensions, and they are God's to set.

corruption_summary: Ezekiel's measured temple is pressed into a timetable for a rebuilt sacrificial house, or waved away as meaningless detail, and in both cases the stated purpose of the measuring is lost.
corruption_paragraphs: Dispensational premillennialism reads Ezekiel 40 to 48 as the blueprint of a literal millennial temple with restored animal sacrifices. The dictionary rejects dispensationalism as a nineteenth-century novelty absent from every Reformation confession, and rejects this reading in particular because Hebrews forecloses it: there remaineth no more offering for sin, and to reinstitute the shadow would be to deny the finished work. The opposite error treats the chapters as unintelligible and skips them.

Ezekiel himself gives the purpose, and it is neither a construction schedule nor nothing. The house is shewn that Israel may be ashamed of their iniquities and measure the pattern. The exact wideness between the chambers preaches that God, not the worshipper, sets the dimensions of holiness; and the vision ends with the river and the name of the city, The LORD is there. Christ is the temple, His body the house, and His people the measured dwelling of God by the Spirit.

pos: adv. (toward the seat; in the phrase to the mercy seatward, facing the mercy seat)
etymology: A compound of seat and the directional suffix -ward, Old English -weard, meaning turned toward, as in homeward and heavenward. The Hebrew is simply el, toward.
biblical_def: The making of the ark is described twice, and the second account closes with the direction of the cherubim's faces: “And the cherubims spread out their wings on high, and covered with their wings over the mercy seat, with their faces one to another; even to the mercy seatward were the faces of the cherubims” (Exodus 37:9). Seatward means toward the seat, and the detail is doctrine. The cherubim do not face outward as guards, nor upward as worshippers of the air; they face down and in, toward the blood-sprinkled lid of the ark. What they look at is the place where atonement is made. God had told Moses where He would meet with Israel: “And there I will meet with thee, and I will commune with thee from above the mercy seat, from between the two cherubims which are upon the ark of the testimony” (Exodus 25:22). Beneath the lid lay the broken law; above it the blood; between the cherubim the glory. The writer to the Hebrews gathers it in a phrase: “And over it the cherubims of glory shadowing the mercyseat” (Hebrews 9:5). Peter says the angels desire to look into these things. The gaze of heaven is turned toward the propitiation.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): -WARD, a termination denoting direction, as in homeward, heavenward; SEATWARD, toward the seat.
webster_full: WARD, a termination signifying direction or tendency to, as in homeward, heavenward.
SEAT, n. That on which one sits; the place of sitting.
MERCY-SEAT, the propitiatory; the lid or covering of the ark of the covenant.
Exodus 37:9 says the faces of the cherubims were to the mercy seatward.
Hebrew el, toward.
scriptures: Exo 37:9
And the cherubims spread out their wings on high, and covered with their wings over the mercy seat, with their faces one to another; even to the mercy seatward were the faces of the cherubims.

And there I will meet with thee, and I will commune with thee from above the mercy seat, from between the two cherubims which are upon the ark of the testimony, of all things which I will give thee in commandment unto the children of Israel.
Heb 9:5
And over it the cherubims of glory shadowing the mercyseat; of which we cannot now speak particularly.
corruption_summary: Propitiation is removed from the centre of the atonement, so that the mercy seat becomes a symbol of divine kindness in general and the blood that was sprinkled on it is treated as primitive.
corruption_paragraphs: A long line of liberal and now progressive-evangelical writers reject penal substitution, calling the sprinkled blood of the mercy seat a vestige of primitive religion and offering instead a moral-influence or Christ-the-Victor account standing alone. The objection is not new, and it always requires the same move: the hilasterion, the propitiatory, must be reinterpreted as mere expiation or as a picture of God's solidarity with sufferers.

Exodus 37:9 answers with the direction of two golden faces. The cherubim look at the place of blood. Paul says Christ was set forth a propitiation through faith in His blood, using the very word the Greek Old Testament uses for the mercy seat, and declares the purpose: that God might be just, and the justifier of him which believeth. Substitutionary penal atonement is not an awkward strand within the doctrine; it is the thing the cherubim were made to stare at.
roots_summary: Seat plus the directional -ward; Exodus 37:9 turns the cherubim's faces to the mercy seatward.
roots_lines: Old English -weard, turned toward, as in homeward and heavenward.
Hebrew el, toward.
Exodus 37:9 is the only occurrence of seatward in the Authorized Version.
The cherubim face down and in, toward the place of atonement.
Hebrews 9:5 calls them the cherubims of glory shadowing the mercyseat.
usage: even to the mercy seatward were the faces of the cherubims
fixes the gaze of heaven upon the place of propitiation
preserves a compound the modern versions dissolve

pos: n. (a threshing floor; the flat place where grain is trodden out)
etymology: A compound of threshing, from Old English therscan, to beat or tread out grain, and place. The Hebrew goren is a threshing floor, usually a flat exposed rock on a height where the wind could carry the chaff.
biblical_def: At the end of David's plague the angel of judgment stops at a particular spot: “And when the angel stretched out his hand upon Jerusalem to destroy it, the LORD repented him of the evil, and said to the angel that destroyed the people, It is enough: stay now thine hand. And the angel of the LORD was by the threshingplace of Araunah the Jebusite” (2 Samuel 24:16). A threshingplace is a threshing floor, the flat rock on a hill where sheaves were trodden and the chaff winnowed away. The word is used here and the ordinary form threshingfloor two verses later, when the prophet brings the command: “Go up, rear an altar unto the LORD in the threshingfloor of Araunah the Jebusite” (2 Samuel 24:18). David bought the site and refused to offer what cost him nothing. And that purchased floor became the holiest ground in Israel: “Then Solomon began to build the house of the LORD at Jerusalem in mount Moriah... in the place that David had prepared in the threshingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite” (2 Chronicles 3:1). Where the sword was stayed, a temple was built; the place of threshing became the place of sacrifice.
webster_summary: Webster (1828): THRESHING-FLOOR, a floor or area on which grain is beaten out; THRESH, to beat out grain from the ear.
webster_full: THRESHING-FLOOR, n. A floor or area, on which grain is beaten out.
THRESH, v.t. To beat out grain from the husk or ear.
PLACE, n. A particular portion of space; a locality.
Hebrew goren, a threshing floor, commonly a flat rock on a height.
2 Samuel 24:16 says the angel stood by the threshingplace of Araunah the Jebusite.
scriptures: And when the angel stretched out his hand upon Jerusalem to destroy it, the LORD repented him of the evil, and said to the angel that destroyed the people, It is enough: stay now thine hand. And the angel of the LORD was by the threshingplace of Araunah the Jebusite.
And Gad came that day to David, and said unto him, Go up, rear an altar unto the LORD in the threshingfloor of Araunah the Jebusite.

Then Solomon began to build the house of the LORD at Jerusalem in mount Moriah, where the LORD appeared unto David his father, in the place that David had prepared in the threshingfloor of Ornan the Jebusite.
corruption_summary: The plague narrative is reduced to a cultic legend explaining why the temple stood where it did, and the costly purchase of the site is detached from the doctrine of acceptable sacrifice.
corruption_paragraphs: Critical treatments commonly read 2 Samuel 24 as an etiological story composed to legitimate the temple site, with the angel and the plague as literary furniture. The dictionary holds the narrative as history: David sinned in numbering the people, the LORD sent judgment, the angel was stayed at a named man's threshing floor, and the site was bought for silver at a stated price.

What the critical reading costs is the doctrine David himself states. Offered the floor as a gift, he refuses: he will not offer unto the LORD of that which costs him nothing. The place where judgment halted was purchased, an altar reared, the plague stayed, and in time the temple built. Mount Moriah had already seen a father, a son and a substitute. The threshingplace is one of the great geographical sermons of Scripture: judgment stayed, a price paid, and the house of God built on the spot.
roots_summary: Threshing plus place; Hebrew goren, a threshing floor; 2 Samuel 24:16 halts the angel at Araunah's threshingplace.
roots_lines: Old English therscan, to beat out grain, gives thresh and threshing.
Hebrew goren, a threshing floor, usually flat rock on a height.
2 Samuel 24:16 is the only occurrence of threshingplace in the Authorized Version.
Two verses later the ordinary form threshingfloor is used of the same spot.
2 Chronicles 3:1 builds the temple on that purchased floor in mount Moriah.
usage: the angel of the LORD was by the threshingplace of Araunah the Jebusite
names the spot where judgment was stayed and the temple later built
ties winnowing imagery to the place of sacrifice
